title: Paul Francis Webster and lyricists' credit
summary: They discuss Webster's irate letter about credit for The Shadow of Your Smile and lyricists getting short shrift, from Hammerstein to Ira Gershwin and Mercer.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It's interesting, in the 60s as you probably know Clare Fischer recorded the tune on an album of his called, Songs for Rainy Day Lovers…

And there was a review of it in, DownBeat around that time and they talked about Johnny Mandel's, “The Shadow of Your Smile.” And Paul Francis Webster wrote an irate letter to DownBeat complaining about when you talk about these tunes you should list – he said, “Johnny Mandel did not write, “The Shadow of Your Smile,” however Johnny Mandel and Paul Francis Webster did,” and he talked about…
He’s right, all I wrote was [sings melody of “The Shadow of Your Smile”]
It was Paul that came up with that title.
And he had every, yeah, and he had every reason to be irate. It was like the old story with…
Oscar Hammerstein and, “Ol’ Man River,” Jerome Kerns, “Ol’ Man River,” and Dorothy Hammerstein got furious she said, “Mr. Kern wrote da-da-dada, Oscar wrote, “Ol’ Man River.””
It’s absolutely true, lyricists always get short shrift, with very few exceptions.
And through the ages they have, Gershwin’s it’s always George it's never Ira and Ira was invaluable to George, as great as George was and believe me he was great.
Johnny Mercer might be the only exception because I've heard tunes referred to as Johnny Mercer tunes that were tunes where he actually wrote the lyric but not the music.
And he wrote wonderful music when he wrote it. All of Johnny Mercer's music that he ever wrote was very good, as musical and natural as could be. I love his songs when he wrote both.
Yeah, a little later on I have a whole list of lyricists that you’ve associated with…
